basis: Ushojo alu potato matches the regional ālu tuber name, with initial stress. The modern American crop referent reflects semantic transfer/contact, not uninterrupted potato vocabulary from Old Indo-Aryan; retain the tuber-word family but exclude a strict inherited crop-accent test.

Ushojo aẓo rain matches abhrá through the characteristic bhr-to-retroflex-sibilant development and final o. Initial stress is explicit and can be compared at the syllable level with Shina aẓo; old cluster simplification did not obligatorily give a written long vowel here.

Ushojo mũẓo rat matches mūṣa but is explicitly stressed on the FINAL o, unlike Brokskat initial-stressed mauzi. This suggests a distinct accentual/inflectional class or a source problem; do not assume all final o endings are unaccented.

Brokskat loodo and Ushojo leolo red match the lōhila red set, with Brokskat d versus Ushojo l and different contraction. Ushojo stresses the second vowel group in leolo, supplying precontraction evidence relevant to Gilgit loólyo; Brokskat is initially stressed. Vowel sequence interpretation remains explicit.

Ushojo tanol rice matches taṇḍulá with cluster simplification but has INITIAL stress. Its unextended disyllabic result is a counterexample to a universal final-long/root-final attraction account; quantity and regional borrowing require separate investigation.

Ushojo aŋguṭi ring matches the aṅguṣṭhiya finger-ring derivative, with final stress and a feminine i ending. It is not the same formation as aṅguli finger, independently distinguishing suffix accent from the finger noun's medial stress.

Brokskat sin and Ushojo suṇḍu river match síndhu; Ushojo retains more of the nasal-stop sequence and final vowel than Brokskat. Neither source token marks stress, so the segmental correspondence is not a demonstrated accent correspondence.

Brokskat šaltaa roof plausibly matches the śalākā/stick-to-roof set and Shina šalto, but the t and final aa require derivational clarification. Its initial stress is documented; retain the family link provisionally rather than treating šalākā as the exact immediate input.

Ushojo niari root matches the nāḍī/nēṛi root/tubular-organ family through intervocalic retroflex weakening and fronting. Final stress is explicit; unequal ia must remain an unresolved sequence, not automatically a long vowel.

Brokskat stored ḍiḍuuro round is a candidate for piṇḍara/piṇḍūro round, but its initial consonant and accent may be transcriptional displacement from a neighboring table column. Exclude until the printed Brokskat cell verifies that this is actually its form.

Ushojo luni salt matches lavaṇá after medial contraction and final i formation, with initial stress. The final i cell and loss of the old three-syllable structure prevent direct comparison with the Sanskrit final syllable alone.

Ushojo sigal sand matches síkatā/sigal but stresses the SECOND syllable, whereas Shina survey sigal can be initial. The final l extension and voiced velar need formation analysis; retain the accent difference as a residual rather than silently transferring Shina stress.

Brokskat raazis say matches the ra/rāp speaking root plus recurring zis/is citation morphology. Rápati versus rásati remains a competing ultimate analysis, so this is a speaking-root family comparison and not a test of the Sanskrit finite headword's exact accent.

Ushojo kenege scratch (past) plausibly contains the kaṇḍū/khān scratch root with e-grade and past eg morphology, but aspiration loss and the extended suffix need paradigmatic confirmation. Keep it out of strict old-present accent predictions.

Brokskat bii seed matches bī́ja through j loss and contraction. The stored acute is only stress at most in this source, pending the printed cell; it is not evidence of an independently transcribed Brokskat early mora.

Ushojo kirnino sell (future) preserves the krīṇ buying/selling root and nasal, with future/citation morphology. The sell sense is independently paralleled in Palula; stress on ni belongs to the actual modern paradigm and cannot be read as direct finite krīṇāti inheritance.
Brokskat sat and Ushojo saat seven match saptá after pt simplification. Their contrasting written length is an independent quantity observation; neither has a marked mora accent in these tokens.

Brokskat sattooṣ and Ushojo sataš seventeen retain the seven-plus-ten compound and stress its second syllable. The DB Brokskat acute cannot itself specify mora, but the apostrophe is consistent with final syllable stress; verify the printed cell.

Brokskat tino and Ushojo tinu sharp match tīkṣṇá with kṣṇ reduction and final o/u adjective endings. Both are explicitly initial-stressed, and neither source writes a long root in these tokens; shortening and ending formation are independent of the old oxytone accent.
Ushojo sʌ she is identical to its he pronoun and belongs to the sa demonstrative base with gender neutralization. No distinct feminine lexical accent is marked.

Ushojo khuṭo short matches the khuṭṭa defective/short family; the same source also uses khuṭo for lame/dwarf, linked provisionally3941. These overlapping old headword assignments must not be counted as independent lexical accent evidence for one modern form.

Ushojo uŋgi sickle matches aṅka hook/sickle derivatives with a rounded vowel and final i. Initial stress is explicit; morphological gender/cell and the velar voicing remain part of the formation comparison.

Ushojo paru sieve matches the paripavana/paruuṇ winnowing family, but lacks the final nasal and has INITIAL stress versus Palula parúuṇ. The shorter formation or different final vowel/cell may explain the accent; retain the discrepancy and require a paradigm before deciding.
Ushojo sas sister preserves the two sibilants of svásr̥, unlike bhaginī-derived sister names. It is an unmarked short monosyllable and cannot independently establish early/late mora.

Brokskat bɨɨs and Ushojo be sit match the upaviś/bai sitting root through contraction, with Brokskat citation s. Ushojo stored down! is English gloss spillover; only be is lexical. These are root-family/citation comparisons, not the old finite formation unchanged.
Brokskat saa and Ushojo ṣa six match ṣáṣ with final sibilant loss. Brokskat length differs from Ushojo, and neither token supplies a mora accent mark.

Brokskat sobeš and Ushojo ṣeš sixteen belong to ṣóḍaśa with differing contraction/analogy. Brokskat has initial stress, unlike its seventeen; Ushojo is now monosyllabic and cannot test original syllable accent. Exact Brokskat consonant reading remains pending.
Ushojo com skin matches cárman with medial cluster/final syllable reduction and rounded vowel; no accent is marked.
Ushojo asman sky is the same Persian āsmān regional loan as Shina asman, with final stress; preserve the contact family and exclude inherited Indo-Aryan accent prediction.

Brokskat sas sleep plausibly contains the s/su sleep root and recurring citation s, comparable with svap/sup descendants. Exact stem vowel and paradigm are uncertain, so this is a root-family link only, not an accent test of svápati.

Ushojo d(h)um smoke matches dhūmá, with explicitly optional aspiration in the transcription. Parentheses do not represent a second word; the token lacks a marked accent and written length, so its quantity outcome remains source-limited.
